text:
Day 4/30 – How dbt Works (Simple Breakdown)

Most people overcomplicate dbt… 
But the workflow is actually very simple 👇 

1️⃣ Write SQL models 
2️⃣ dbt builds dependency DAG 
3️⃣ Transform data inside warehouse 
4️⃣ Test & validate data quality 
5️⃣ Deliver analytics-ready data 

💡 Why dbt is powerful: 
✔ No data movement (runs in warehouse) 
✔ SQL-first approach 
✔ Built-in testing & documentation 
✔ Version-controlled pipelines 

👉 In one line: 
dbt = SQL + Automation + Testing + Documentation

If you're working with Snowflake, BigQuery, or Redshift… 
dbt is not optional anymore.

headline: Data Engineer @ TCS | Building Scalable Data Pipelines on Cloud | 41K+ Strong LinkedIn Network | Cloud | Marketing | 40M+ impressions |Analytics | Growth|Sustainability |Open for collabs
text:
Most Data Engineer candidates make the same mistake.

They master SQL.
They learn PySpark.
…and still fail interviews.

I’ve seen this happen again and again.
The problem?
👉 Lack of scenario-based thinking.
Let me tell you what actually gets you hired 

👇
🔹 1. Can you explain a pipeline end-to-end?
Not just tools.
But clearly: Raw → Clean → Warehouse
Incremental logic
Monitoring
Because interviewers test clarity, not complexity.

🔹 2. Pipeline suddenly becomes slow… what will you do?
Strong candidates don’t panic.
They debug step-by-step:
→ Ingestion / Transform / Load
→ Check Spark UI, logs, skew
→ Fix only the bottleneck

🔹 3. Incremental Loads (real-world favorite)
→ Watermark (last_updated)
→ CDC handling
→ Reprocess small overlap

🔹 4. Late arriving data?
This is where many fail.
→ Reprocess last 1–3 days
→ Make pipelines idempotent
→ Track audit columns

🔹 5. Spark OutOfMemory error?
Don’t just increase memory ❌
Check:
→ Wide transformations
→ Data skew
→ Large joins
Fix:
→ Repartition
→ Broadcast joins

🔹 6. Data mismatch issue?
Validate layer by layer:
Source → Raw → Transform → Warehouse

🔹 7. Data skew in Spark?
Detect imbalance.
Fix with:
→ Salting
→ Repartition

💡 Here’s the truth:
Companies don’t hire you for what you know.

They hire you for how you think.
If you're preparing for Data Engineering interviews, focus on scenarios like these.

text:
Cleared my SQL round with this one sheet 🔥


They asked 6 topics in one interview.
I had revised all 6 the night before.

Here is the complete SQL breakdown ↓

→ DDL vs DML vs DCL vs TCL

• DDL - CREATE, ALTER, DROP, TRUNCATE
 ↳ Rollback - No | Data after DROP - Lost

• DML - INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, SELECT
 ↳ Rollback - Yes | DML can be rolled back

• DCL - GRANT, REVOKE
 ↳ Controls who accesses what

• TCL - COMMIT, ROLLBACK, SAVEPOINT
 ↳ Controls when changes are permanent

→ SQL Execution Order

• FROM → get the table first
• WHERE → filter rows
• GROUP BY → group filtered rows
• HAVING → filter groups
• SELECT → pick columns
• ORDER BY → sort result
• LIMIT → restrict rows

WHERE runs before SELECT
Alias not allowed in WHERE - this is why

→ Joins in One Line

• INNER - matching rows only
• LEFT - all left + matched right
• RIGHT - all right + matched left
• FULL OUTER - all rows both sides
• SELF - table joined to itself

→ Window Functions

• ROW_NUMBER - unique rank, no ties
• RANK - same rank, yes gaps
• DENSE_RANK - same rank, no gaps
• LAG - previous row value
• LEAD - next row value

All work with PARTITION BY and ORDER BY
No rows are lost unlike GROUP BY

→ NULL Handling

• COALESCE - returns first non-null value
• NULLIF - returns null if two values are equal
• COUNT(*) counts nulls
• COUNT(col) ignores nulls

→ One Line Summary

DDL = structure
DML = data
DCL = access
TCL = transactions
WHERE = rows | HAVING = groups

Most candidates know SELECT.
Very few know the execution order under pressure. 💪

↳ Save this before your next SQL interview.

text:
Here are 12 SQL queries that turn raw data into business insights:
(Save this - these are the ones that actually matter in real work)

Every business question has a SQL query behind it.
The analysts who get promoted are not the ones who know the most syntax.

They are the ones who know which query to write for which business problem - instantly.
Here are 12 you need to have memorized 👇

1. Total Revenue Calculation
-- Quick snapshot of overall business performance and revenue health

2. Daily Sales Trend
-- Tracks day by day performance to spot peaks, drops, and patterns

3. Top Selling Products
-- Highlights products driving the highest demand and revenue contribution

4. Revenue by Category
-- Shows which categories are performing best across the business

5. Customer Lifetime Value
-- Identifies high-value customers for retention and personalized marketing

6. Average Order Value
-- Measures how much customers spend per transaction on average

7. Monthly Revenue Growth
-- Tracks growth trends and seasonal patterns over time

8. Repeat Customers
-- Finds loyal customers contributing to recurring revenue

9. New vs Returning Customers
-- Segments users into new and returning for targeted strategies

10. Conversion Rate
-- Measures how efficiently visitors convert into paying customers

11. Top Customers by Revenue
-- Pinpoints your most valuable customers driving major revenue

12. Churned Customers
-- Identifies inactive users who may need re-engagement campaigns

Here is what I tell every analyst on my team:
Knowing these 12 queries is not enough.

You need to know the business question behind each one.

Because a stakeholder will never ask you "can you write query number 7."
They will ask "why is revenue declining month over month?"
And you need to know immediately which query answers that — and what to do with the result.

SQL is the easy part.
Business thinking is the skill.
Which of these do you use most in your daily work?

author: Rahul G
headline: Senior Data Engineer at Vanguard
text:
𝐎𝐋𝐀𝐏 𝐯𝐬 𝐎𝐋𝐓𝐏

Every data engineering interview asks this.
Most candidates give a half-answer. Here's the complete breakdown. 📌

𝐎𝐋𝐓𝐏 — 𝐎𝐧𝐥𝐢𝐧𝐞 𝐓𝐫𝐚𝐧𝐬𝐚𝐜𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐏𝐫𝐨𝐜𝐞𝐬𝐬𝐢𝐧𝐠
→ Purpose: Record and manage real-time transactions
→ Queries: Short fast reads/writes (INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE)
→ Data volume: Gigabytes — optimized for speed per transaction
→ Schema: Highly normalized (3NF) to avoid redundancy
→ Users: Backend apps, microservices
→ Examples: MySQL, PostgreSQL, Oracle
 
𝐎𝐋𝐀𝐏 — 𝐎𝐧𝐥𝐢𝐧𝐞 𝐀𝐧𝐚𝐥𝐲𝐭𝐢𝐜𝐚𝐥 𝐏𝐫𝐨𝐜𝐞𝐬𝐬𝐢𝐧𝐠
→ Purpose: Analyze large volumes of historical data
→ Queries: Complex aggregations, window functions, multi-table joins
→ Data volume: Terabytes to petabytes
→ Schema: Denormalized — star or snowflake schema for query speed
→ Users: Analysts, BI tools, data scientists
→ Examples: Snowflake, BigQuery, Redshift, ClickHouse
 
The key insight most people miss:
OLTP is optimized for writing fast. OLAP is optimized for reading at scale.
 
And here's why data engineers exist:
We move data FROM OLTP systems INTO OLAP systems. That transformation is the ETL/ELT pipeline you build every day.
